```{python}
economy_df = pd.read_csv('../data/global_economy.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])


def exports(country):
    """One country's exports (% of GDP) in the unique_id / ds / y layout statsforecast expects."""
    return (economy_df.query("unique_id == @country")[["unique_id", "ds", "Exports"]]
            .rename(columns={"Exports": "y"}).dropna().reset_index(drop=True))


def simulate(ar=(), ma=(), n=200, seed=1):
    """A sample path of the ARMA process y_t = sum(ar) y_{t-i} + e_t + sum(ma) e_{t-i}."""
    process = ArmaProcess(np.r_[1, -np.asarray(ar)], np.r_[1, np.asarray(ma)])
    return process.generate_sample(n, distrvs=np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal)
```

# Where this fits

## Five weeks, one question left open {.smaller}

| Week | What the model describes |
|---|---|
| 2 | The series as trend + season + remainder |
| 4 | A level, a slope and a season that update as data arrive |
| 5 | $y$ as a function of the calendar and of outside predictors |

. . .

Every one of them describes the **shape** of the series and treats what is left over as noise. Week
5 ended on the leftover that was not noise: residuals whose ACF said *this week's error looks like
last week's*.

[ARIMA turns that around: it models the autocorrelation itself, and lets the shape follow from it.]{.hi}

## What this lecture is for {.smaller}

1. **Stationarity and differencing** — the one transformation ARIMA cannot do without, and the tests
   that tell you how much of it to apply.
2. **AR, MA, ARIMA** — three building blocks, and the surprise that you have already used several of
   them under other names.
3. **Specifying a model by hand** from the ACF and PACF, and checking it against `AutoARIMA`.
4. **Forecasting**, including where the prediction intervals come from.

Part 2, next week, adds seasonal ARIMA terms and puts ARIMA against ETS.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading

[FPP3 ch. 9, §9.1–9.8](https://otexts.com/fpp3/arima.html) ·
[FPP the Pythonic Way, ch. 9](https://otexts.com/fpppy/nbs/09-arima.html)
:::

# Stationarity

## What stationary means {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition

$y_t$ is **stationary** if for every $s$ the distribution of $(y_t, \dots, y_{t+s})$ does not depend
on $t$.
:::

In words: pick any window of the series, slide it along, and the statistical picture does not change.
In practice that means

- **no trend** — the mean does not drift;
- **constant variance** — the swings are the same size early and late;
- **nothing predictable in the long run** — no seasonality, because a season tells you where the
  series will be at a given time.

::: {.callout-important}
**Cycles are allowed.** A cycle of irregular length — a business cycle, a commodity boom — does not
tell you *when* the next peak comes, so a series with cycles can be stationary. Seasonality can't be,
because its period is fixed.
:::

## Which of these are stationary? {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: stationarity-quiz
#| fig-align: center
gafa = pd.read_csv('../data/gafa_stock.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
google = gafa.query("unique_id == 'GOOG_Close' and ds.dt.year == 2015").reset_index(drop=True)
eggs = pd.read_csv('../data/egg_prices.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
beer = pd.read_csv('../data/aus_production.csv', parse_dates=["ds"]).query("ds.dt.year >= 1992")
employment = pd.read_csv('../data/us_employment.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
retail = employment.query("unique_id == 'Retail Trade' and ds.dt.year >= 1990").reset_index(drop=True)
egypt = exports("Egypt, Arab Rep.")

panels = {
    "a": ("Google closing price, 2015", google.ds, google.y, 1),
    "b": ("Google daily change, 2015", google.ds[1:], google.y.diff()[1:], 1),
    "c": ("US egg prices, annual", eggs.ds, eggs.y, 1),
    "d": ("Australian beer production, quarterly", beer.ds, beer.Beer, 4),
    "e": ("Egyptian exports, % of GDP, annual", egypt.ds, egypt.y, 1),
    "f": ("US retail employment, monthly", retail.ds, retail.y, 12),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 5.6))
for ax, (key, (title, x, y, _)) in zip(axes.flat, panels.items()):
    ax.plot(x, y, color=slate, linewidth=0.9)
    ax.set_title(f"({key}) {title}", fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
plt.show()
```

## The answer, computed {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
rows = []
for key, (title, _, y, m) in panels.items():
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    D = nsdiffs(y, period=m) if m > 1 else 0
    y_s = y[m:] - y[:-m] if D else y
    rows.append({"series": f"({key})", "m": m,
                 "seasonal diffs D": D,
                 "first diffs d": ndiffs(y_s)})
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

- **(b)** and **(e)** need no differencing: the
  changes in a stock price, and a series whose ups and downs are cycles of irregular length.
- **(a)** and **(c)** wander, so they need a first difference; **(d)** and **(f)** have a season,
  so they need a seasonal one.
- `nsdiffs` and `ndiffs` are the tests behind `AutoARIMA`. We open them up later in this section.

## The ACF says it too {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: google-acf
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4))
plot_acf(google.y, lags=30, zero=False, ax=axes[0], auto_ylims=True,
         title="Google closing price: ACF")
plot_acf(google.y.diff().dropna(), lags=30, zero=False, ax=axes[1], auto_ylims=True,
         title="Daily change: ACF")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
change = google.y.diff().dropna()
print(f"price:  r1 = {google.y.autocorr(1):.2f}")
print(f"change: r1 = {change.autocorr(1):+.2f}   "
      f"Ljung-Box (10 lags) p = {acorr_ljungbox(change, lags=[10])['lb_pvalue'].iloc[0]:.2f}")
```

- Non-stationary: the ACF decays **slowly**, and $r_1$ is large and positive.
- Stationary: the ACF drops to zero **quickly**. The daily changes pass Ljung-Box, so they are white
  noise. That makes the price a **random walk**, and the best forecast of it is the naive forecast
  from Week 1.

# Differencing

## First and second differences {.smaller}

Differencing removes a changing level. The new series is the **change** from one observation to the
next:

$$
y'_t = y_t - y_{t-1}
$$

It has $T-1$ observations. If the changes still trend, difference again:

$$
y''_t = y'_t - y'_{t-1} = (y_t - y_{t-1}) - (y_{t-1} - y_{t-2}) = y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}
$$

That leaves $T-2$ observations, and it models the **change in the change**. In practice you almost
never need to go beyond second order.

## Seasonal differences {.smaller}

The change from the **same season last year**:

$$
y'_t = y_t - y_{t-m}, \qquad m = \text{the seasonal period}
$$

- With $m = 12$ this is "this January minus last January". It takes out a fixed seasonal pattern.
- If the seasonal difference still wanders, take a first difference of it as well:

$$
y''_t = (y_t - y_{t-m}) - (y_{t-1} - y_{t-m-1}) = y_t - y_{t-1} - y_{t-m} + y_{t-m-1}
$$

::: {.callout-note}
A difference needs to mean something. A first difference is the change since last period, and a
seasonal difference is the change since last year. Differences at other lags, say lag 3 on annual
data, usually have no sensible interpretation.
:::

## US retail employment, differenced {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: retail-differences
#| fig-align: center
y_r = retail.set_index("ds").y
steps = {"raw": y_r,
         "seasonal difference (lag 12)": y_r.diff(12),
         "seasonal + first difference": y_r.diff(12).diff()}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(13, 6.2), width_ratios=[2.2, 1])
for (name, s), (ax_l, ax_r) in zip(steps.items(), axes):
    ax_l.plot(s.index, s, color=slate, linewidth=0.9)
    ax_l.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
    plot_acf(s.dropna(), lags=36, zero=False, ax=ax_r, auto_ylims=True, title="")
    ax_r.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))
fig.suptitle("Thousands of employees, 1990–2019")
plt.show()
```

## Which difference, and how many {.smaller}

- **Seasonal first** when the season is strong. The seasonal difference may already be stationary, and
  here it is: `ndiffs` returned 0 after the seasonal difference. Order does not matter
  mathematically, since $(1-B)(1-B^{12}) = (1-B^{12})(1-B)$, but it decides whether you stop after
  one. The ACF of the seasonal difference still decays slowly, but KPSS does not reject, so the
  remaining persistence is left to the AR terms rather than to a second difference.
- **Do not over-difference.** Differencing a series that is already white noise does not leave white
  noise:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
twice = change.diff().dropna()
print(f"Google changes:          r1 = {change.autocorr(1):+.2f}")
print(f"changes, differenced:    r1 = {twice.autocorr(1):+.2f}   (theory: -0.50)")
```

If $y_t = \varepsilon_t$, then $y'_t = \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1}$, and that series has
$\rho_1 = -0.5$. **A large negative spike at lag 1 after differencing is the sign you went one step too far.**

## Unit root tests {.smaller}

Tests that decide whether to difference. They come in two kinds, with **opposite null hypotheses**:

| Test | $H_0$ | Small $p$ means |
|---|---|---|
| ADF (augmented Dickey–Fuller) | non-stationary | stationary, do not difference |
| **KPSS** | **stationary** | non-stationary, **difference** |

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
pd.DataFrame([
    {"series": name,
     "ADF p": adfuller(s)[1],
     "KPSS p": kpss(s, nlags="auto")[1]}
    for name, s in [("price", google.y), ("change", change)]
]).round(3)
```

Both tests agree on Google. `statsmodels` clips the KPSS $p$ to $[0.01, 0.10]$, the range of its
lookup table.

`AutoARIMA` uses **KPSS**. It differences only when the data reject stationarity, so by default it
leans towards *not* differencing.

## The tests in one call {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
y_ret = retail.y.to_numpy(float)
print("ndiffs, Google price:              ", ndiffs(google.y.to_numpy(float)))
print("nsdiffs, retail employment (m=12):  ", nsdiffs(y_ret, period=12))
print("ndiffs after the seasonal difference:", ndiffs(y_ret[12:] - y_ret[:-12]))
```

- `ndiffs` applies KPSS again and again: difference, test, repeat, up to $d = 2$.
- `nsdiffs` uses the **seasonal strength** from Week 2:

$$
F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)
$$

and takes one seasonal difference if $F_S > 0.64$. You computed $F_S$ in Lab 3, and every Track B
series was screened on it (the issue rule is $F_S \ge 0.6$), so expect $D = 1$ on your own series.

# Backshift notation

## The operator $B$ {.smaller}

$$
B y_t = y_{t-1}, \qquad B^2 y_t = y_{t-2}, \qquad B^{12} y_t = y_{t-12}
$$

Differences become polynomials in $B$, and polynomials multiply:

| Operation | Written as |
|---|---|
| First difference $y_t - y_{t-1}$ | $(1-B)\,y_t$ |
| Second-**order** difference $y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}$ | $(1-B)^2\,y_t$ |
| $d$-th order difference | $(1-B)^d\,y_t$ |
| Seasonal difference $y_t - y_{t-m}$ | $(1-B^m)\,y_t$ |
| Seasonal then first | $(1-B)(1-B^m)\,y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} - y_{t-m} + y_{t-m-1}$ |

::: {.callout-warning}
$(1-B)^2$ is a second-*order* difference. $1-B^2$ is a *lag-2* difference, $y_t - y_{t-2}$. They are
different things.
:::

# Autoregressive models

## AR($p$) {.smaller}

$$
y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \dots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{white noise}
$$

A regression of $y_t$ on **its own lags**. It is the Week 5 model with the lags of $y$ as the only
predictors.

```{python}
#| label: ar-examples
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4), sharey=True)
axes[0].plot(18 / 1.8 + simulate(ar=[-0.8], n=100, seed=7), color=slate)
axes[0].set_title(r"AR(1): $y_t = 18 - 0.8\,y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$")
axes[1].plot(20 + simulate(ar=[1.3, -0.7], n=100, seed=7), color=turquoise)
axes[1].set_title(r"AR(2): $y_t = 8 + 1.3\,y_{t-1} - 0.7\,y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("t")
plt.show()
```

The left series flips sign every step. The right one moves in slow waves. Two coefficients are enough
to make a cycle.

## AR(1): what $\phi_1$ does {.smaller}

$$
y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t
$$

| $\phi_1$ | $c$ | The process is |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | white noise |
| 1 | 0 | a **random walk**: naive forecasts |
| 1 | $\neq 0$ | a random walk **with drift**: the drift method |
| $\lvert\phi_1\rvert < 1$ | any | stationary, pulled back to its mean |
| $< 0$ | any | oscillating around the mean |

For $|\phi_1| < 1$ the mean is not $c$:

$$
\mu = c + \phi_1\mu \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu = \frac{c}{1-\phi_1}
$$

[Two of the four Week 1 benchmarks are AR(1) models with $\phi_1 = 1$.]{.hi}

## Stationarity conditions {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: ar2-triangle
#| fig-align: center
phi1 = np.linspace(-2, 2, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.4))
ax.fill([-2, 2, 0], [-1, -1, 1], color=turquoise, alpha=0.18, label="stationary")
ax.fill_between(phi1, -1, -phi1 ** 2 / 4, color=red_pink, alpha=0.18,
                label=r"complex roots: cycles ($\phi_1^2 + 4\phi_2 < 0$)")
ax.plot([-2, 2, 0, -2], [-1, -1, 1, -1], color=slate, linewidth=1.2)
ax.plot(1.3, -0.7, "o", color=turquoise, markersize=9, label="the AR(2) on the previous slide")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\phi_1$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\phi_2$")
ax.set_xlim(-2.2, 2.2)
ax.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.15)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("AR(2): where the coefficients have to live")
plt.show()
```

- AR(1): $-1 < \phi_1 < 1$. AR(2): inside the triangle, $\ -1 < \phi_2 < 1,\ \phi_1 + \phi_2 < 1,\
  \phi_2 - \phi_1 < 1$.
- In the pink region the forecasts move in **cycles**. For $p \ge 3$ the conditions get complicated,
  and the estimation software enforces them for you.

# Moving average models

## MA($q$) {.smaller}

$$
y_t = c + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2\varepsilon_{t-2} + \dots +
\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}
$$

A regression on **past forecast errors**. You never observe them; the model reconstructs them as it
goes, so this is not literally a regression you can run with OLS.

::: {.callout-important}
Not the moving average of Week 2. That one *smoothed* the series to estimate a trend. This one
*generates* the series from past shocks.
:::

```{python}
#| label: ma-examples
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.0), sharey=True)
axes[0].plot(20 + simulate(ma=[0.8], n=100, seed=3), color=slate)
axes[0].set_title(r"MA(1): $y_t = 20 + \varepsilon_t + 0.8\,\varepsilon_{t-1}$")
axes[1].plot(simulate(ma=[-1, 0.8], n=100, seed=3), color=turquoise)
axes[1].set_title(r"MA(2): $y_t = \varepsilon_t - \varepsilon_{t-1} + 0.8\,\varepsilon_{t-2}$")
plt.show()
```

## An AR(1) is an MA($\infty$) {.smaller}

Substitute the model into itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t
     = \phi_1(\phi_1 y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_{t-1}) + \varepsilon_t \\
    &= \phi_1^2 y_{t-2} + \phi_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t
     = \dots = \varepsilon_t + \phi_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \phi_1^2\varepsilon_{t-2} +
       \phi_1^3\varepsilon_{t-3} + \cdots
\end{aligned}
$$

That works only if $|\phi_1| < 1$, so that $\phi_1^k \to 0$. The same algebra works for any
stationary AR($p$):

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
print("MA weights of AR(1), phi = 0.8:   ", np.round(arma2ma([1, -0.8], [1], lags=6), 3))
print("0.8 ** k:                         ", np.round(0.8 ** np.arange(6), 3))
```

Hold on to these **$\psi$ weights**. The prediction intervals at the end of the lecture are built from
them.

## Invertibility {.smaller}

The reverse is also possible: an MA($q$) can be written as an AR($\infty$), but only if
$|\theta_1| < 1$ (for $q = 1$). Why insist on it? Because **without it, the model is not identified**:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
for theta in (0.5, 2.0):
    acf_theory = ArmaProcess([1], [1, theta]).acf(4)[1:]
    print(f"MA(1) with theta = {theta}:  ACF = {np.round(acf_theory, 3)}")
```

$\rho_1 = \theta/(1+\theta^2)$ takes the same value at $\theta$ and at $1/\theta$. The data cannot tell
the two apart, so we keep the one where recent errors matter more than old ones, $|\theta| < 1$.

- MA(2): $-1 < \theta_2 < 1,\ \theta_1 + \theta_2 > -1,\ \theta_1 - \theta_2 < 1$.
- Beyond that, again, the software enforces it.

# ARIMA

## ARMA, then ARIMA {.smaller}

Put lagged values and lagged errors together:

$$
y'_t = c + \phi_1 y'_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_p y'_{t-p} + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \dots +
\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q} + \varepsilon_t
$$

where $y'_t$ is the series after $d$ differences. This is **ARIMA($p, d, q$)**:

- **AR** — $p$, the number of lagged values;
- **I** — "integrated", $d$, the number of first differences;
- **MA** — $q$, the number of lagged errors.

In backshift notation, ARIMA(1,1,1):

$$
\underbrace{(1 - \phi_1 B)}_{\text{AR(1)}}\ \underbrace{(1 - B)}_{\text{first difference}}\ y_t
\;=\; c + \underbrace{(1 + \theta_1 B)}_{\text{MA(1)}}\ \varepsilon_t
$$

## Models you already know {.smaller}

| ARIMA | Is |
|---|---|
| (0, 0, 0), with $c$ | white noise around a mean: the **mean** method |
| (0, 1, 0), no $c$ | random walk: the **naive** method |
| (0, 1, 0), with $c$ | random walk with drift: the **drift** method |
| ($p$, 0, 0) | AR($p$) |
| (0, 0, $q$) | MA($q$) |
| (0, 1, 1), no $c$ | **simple exponential smoothing**, with $\theta_1 = \alpha - 1$ |

[Three of the four Week 1 benchmarks, and the simplest ETS model, are ARIMA models.]{.hi}

The last row is a claim worth checking.

## SES is ARIMA(0,1,1) {.smaller}

Algeria's exports, the series from the Week 4 lecture:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
y_alg = exports("Algeria").y.to_numpy(float)

ses = AutoETS(season_length=1, model="ANN").fit(y=y_alg)
arima011 = ARIMA(order=(0, 1, 1)).fit(y=y_alg)

alpha = ses.model_["par"][0]
theta = arima011.model_["coef"]["ma1"]
print(f"SES:          alpha = {alpha:.3f}  ->  alpha - 1 = {alpha - 1:+.3f}")
print(f"ARIMA(0,1,1): theta = {theta:+.3f}")
print(f"forecast, SES {ses.predict(h=1)['mean'][0]:.3f}  ARIMA {arima011.predict(h=1)['mean'][0]:.3f}")
```

The two are estimated by different software and from different starting points, so the numbers are
not identical to the last digit. The forecasts agree to two decimals.

What ARIMA adds is that **it does not stop at (0,1,1)**. ETS has a fixed menu of components; ARIMA
lets the data pick any $p$ and $q$.

## Egyptian exports {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
egypt.tail(3)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fit_egy = AutoARIMA().fit(y=egypt.y.to_numpy(float))
coef = fit_egy.model_["coef"]
print(ARIMASummary(fit_egy.model_))
print({k: round(float(v), 3) for k, v in coef.items()},
      f" sigma^2 {fit_egy.model_['sigma2']:.2f}   AICc {fit_egy.model_['aicc']:.2f}")
```

## Reading the fitted model {.smaller}

`statsforecast` reports the **mean** $\mu$ as `intercept`, not the constant $c$. To write the
equation, convert:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
c = coef["intercept"] * (1 - coef["ar1"] - coef["ar2"])
cycle = 2 * np.pi / np.arccos(-coef["ar1"] * (1 - coef["ar2"]) / (4 * coef["ar2"]))
print(f"c = mu (1 - phi1 - phi2) = {c:.2f}")
print(f"phi1^2 + 4 phi2 = {coef['ar1'] ** 2 + 4 * coef['ar2']:+.2f}  ->  average cycle {cycle:.1f} years")
```

$$
y_t = 2.56 + 1.68\,y_{t-1} - 0.80\,y_{t-2} - 0.69\,\varepsilon_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t,
\qquad \hat\sigma = \sqrt{8.05} = 2.84
$$

- $d = 0$: the model treats exports as stationary, pulled back to a mean of
  `{python} f"{coef['intercept']:.1f}"`% of GDP.
- $(\phi_1, \phi_2)$ is in the pink region of the triangle, so the series **cycles**, with an
  average length of about 18 years. Nothing in the data is labelled as a cycle. Two AR coefficients
  are enough to produce one.

## What $c$ and $d$ do to the long run {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: long-run
#| fig-align: center
car = exports("Central African Republic")
y_car = car.y.to_numpy(float)
variants = [("ARIMA(1,0,0), c = 0",  ARIMA(order=(1, 0, 0), include_mean=False)),
            ("ARIMA(1,0,0), c ≠ 0",  ARIMA(order=(1, 0, 0), include_mean=True)),
            ("ARIMA(1,1,0), c = 0",  ARIMA(order=(1, 1, 0))),
            ("ARIMA(1,1,0), c ≠ 0",  ARIMA(order=(1, 1, 0), include_drift=True)),
            ("ARIMA(1,2,0), c = 0",  ARIMA(order=(1, 2, 0)))]
h_long = 60
t_hist = np.arange(len(y_car))
t_fc = np.arange(len(y_car), len(y_car) + h_long)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 5.2), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, model) in zip(axes.flat, variants):
    fc = model.fit(y=y_car).predict(h=h_long, level=[80])
    ax.plot(t_hist, y_car, color=slate, linewidth=0.9)
    ax.plot(t_fc, fc["mean"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8)
    ax.fill_between(t_fc, fc["lo-80"], fc["hi-80"], color=red_pink, alpha=0.15)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
axes[0, 0].set_ylim(-15, 45)
axes.flat[-1].axis("off")
axes.flat[-1].text(0.05, 0.5, "c ≠ 0, d = 2 would give a\nquadratic trend.\n\n"
                   "statsforecast does not allow it,\nand you should not want it.",
                   fontsize=11, va="center")
fig.suptitle("Central African Republic exports, % of GDP: the same AR(1), different c and d")
plt.show()
```

## What $c$ and $d$ do to the long run {.smaller}

| | $c = 0$ | $c \neq 0$ |
|---|---|---|
| $d = 0$ | forecasts go to **zero** | go to the **mean** of the data |
| $d = 1$ | go to a **constant** | follow a **straight line** |
| $d = 2$ | follow a **straight line** | a quadratic trend (never used) |

- The higher $d$, the faster the prediction intervals widen. With $d = 0$ they stop growing.
- Choosing $d$ and $c$ amounts to choosing what the forecast does far ahead. That decision is
  yours, and you should make it on purpose. $p$ and $q$ only shape the first few steps.

# Choosing p and q by eye

## Partial autocorrelation {.smaller}

The ACF at lag $k$ mixes direct and indirect links: $y_t$ is related to $y_{t-2}$ partly *through*
$y_{t-1}$. The **partial** autocorrelation removes the intermediaries.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition

$\alpha_k$ = the coefficient $\phi_k$ in the regression
$y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \dots + \phi_k y_{t-k} + \varepsilon_t$.
:::

That is literally how you can compute it:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
lags = pd.DataFrame({f"lag{j}": egypt.y.shift(j) for j in range(1, 6)})
by_regression = [sm.OLS(egypt.y, sm.add_constant(lags.iloc[:, :k]), missing="drop").fit().params.iloc[-1]
                 for k in range(1, 6)]
print("last coefficient of each regression:", np.round(by_regression, 3))
print("pacf(method='ols'):                 ", np.round(pacf(egypt.y, nlags=5, method="ols")[1:], 3))
```

`plot_pacf` uses a Yule–Walker estimate by default. It gives slightly different numbers but the same
idea, and it is judged against the same $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$ band as the ACF.

## The signatures {.smaller}

| | ACF | PACF |
|---|---|---|
| **AR($p$)** | decays, exponentially or as a damped wave | **cuts off after lag $p$** |
| **MA($q$)** | **cuts off after lag $q$** | decays |
| **ARMA($p, q$)** | decays | decays |

```{python}
#| label: signatures
#| fig-align: center
sims = {"AR(2): 1.3, -0.7": simulate(ar=[1.3, -0.7], n=2000, seed=11),
        "MA(2): -1, 0.8": simulate(ma=[-1, 0.8], n=2000, seed=11)}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 3.9))
for row, (name, y_sim) in zip(axes, sims.items()):
    plot_acf(y_sim, lags=12, zero=False, ax=row[0], auto_ylims=True, title=f"{name}: ACF")
    plot_pacf(y_sim, lags=12, zero=False, ax=row[1], auto_ylims=True, title=f"{name}: PACF")
    for ax in row:
        ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))
plt.show()
```

When both decay, the plots do not give you the order. That is when AICc takes over.

## Egyptian exports: ACF and PACF {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.4))
plot_acf(egypt.y, lags=20, zero=False, ax=axes[0], auto_ylims=True)
plot_pacf(egypt.y, lags=20, zero=False, ax=axes[1], auto_ylims=True)
plt.show()
```

- ACF: decays in a wave, which is the AR shape.
- PACF: significant up to **lag 4**, nothing after. That is an AR(4).

## ARIMA(4,0,0), specified by hand {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fit_400 = ARIMA(order=(4, 0, 0)).fit(y=egypt.y.to_numpy(float))
print(ARIMASummary(fit_400.model_))
print({k: round(float(v), 3) for k, v in fit_400.model_["coef"].items()})
print(f"AICc: ARIMA(4,0,0) {fit_400.model_['aicc']:.2f}   AutoARIMA's ARIMA(2,0,1) {fit_egy.model_['aicc']:.2f}")
```

- The PACF suggested an AR(4), and AutoARIMA found an ARMA(2,1). The two AICc values are **less than
  one unit apart**, so AICc cannot separate them.
- That is normal. **Several specifications fit an autocorrelation structure about equally well**, and
  the ACF/PACF reading gives you one reasonable candidate, not the correct answer.

[By hand and automatic disagreeing is not a failure. It is the situation Week 4 told you how to handle:
shortlist on AICc, decide on a holdout.]{.hi}

# Estimation and order selection

## Estimation and information criteria {.smaller}

The parameters $c, \phi_1, \dots, \phi_p, \theta_1, \dots, \theta_q$ are found by **maximum
likelihood**. For Gaussian errors that is close to minimising $\sum e_t^2$, but the errors depend on the
parameters recursively, so it is numerical optimisation, as for ETS. Different software gives slightly
different estimates.

The orders are chosen with the criteria from Week 4, where $k = 1$ if $c \neq 0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{AIC} &= -2\log L + 2(p+q+k+1) \\
\text{AIC}_c &= \text{AIC} + \frac{2(p+q+k+1)(p+q+k+2)}{T-p-q-k-2} \\
\text{BIC} &= \text{AIC} + [\log T - 2](p+q+k+1)
\end{aligned}
$$

## Two comparisons AICc cannot make {.smaller}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Not across different $d$

$L$ is the likelihood of the **differenced** series. ARIMA(2,1,0) and ARIMA(2,0,0) are fitted to
different data, so their AICc are not comparable. Choose $d$ first, using the tests, and then compare
$p$ and $q$ for that $d$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Not across model families

An ARIMA AICc and an ETS AICc are computed on different terms, so you cannot compare them either. To
put ARIMA against ETS, use a holdout or cross-validation. That is part of next week's lecture.
:::

## How `AutoARIMA` searches {.smaller}

The Hyndman–Khandakar algorithm (JSS, 2008):

1. **Choose $d$** with repeated KPSS tests (`ndiffs`). Choose $D$ with seasonal strength (`nsdiffs`).
2. **Start** from the best AICc among ARIMA(2,$d$,2), (0,$d$,0), (1,$d$,0), (0,$d$,1).
3. **Move**: try $p \pm 1$, $q \pm 1$, both together, and with or without $c$. If a neighbour has a lower
   AICc, it becomes the current model.
4. **Repeat** until no neighbour improves.

It is a **stepwise local search**. It visits a few dozen models instead of every one, so it can stop
at a model that is not the best. `stepwise=False` searches the full grid, which is slower.

## The AICc surface it walks on {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: aicc-surface
#| fig-align: center
grid = pd.DataFrame(index=range(6), columns=range(6), dtype=float)
for p in range(6):
    for q in range(6):
        try:
            grid.loc[p, q] = ARIMA(order=(p, 1, q)).fit(y=y_car).model_["aicc"]
        except Exception:
            pass
step_order = AutoARIMA().fit(y=y_car).model_["arma"]
full_order = AutoARIMA(stepwise=False).fit(y=y_car).model_["arma"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.6))
sns.heatmap(grid - np.nanmin(grid.values), annot=True, fmt=".1f", cmap="mako_r", vmax=10,
            cbar_kws={"label": "AICc above the best"}, ax=ax)
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((step_order[1], step_order[0]), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor=orange, lw=3))
ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((full_order[1], full_order[0]), 1, 1, fill=False, edgecolor=red_pink, lw=3))
ax.set_xlabel("q")
ax.set_ylabel("p")
ax.set_title(f"Central African Republic exports, d = 1: orange = stepwise, "
             f"pink = full search")
plt.show()
```

The stepwise search stopped at ARIMA(`{python} f"{step_order[0]},1,{step_order[1]}"`). The grid's best is
ARIMA(`{python} f"{full_order[0]},1,{full_order[1]}"`). The difference is 0.6 units of AICc, and three
other models are within one unit of the best. The search did not fail. **The surface is flat**, and
on a flat surface the minimum tells you very little.

# The modelling procedure

## By hand, or automatically {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**By hand — what the challenge asks for first**

1. Plot the data; transform if the variance grows.
2. Difference until stationary: `nsdiffs`, then `ndiffs`.
3. Read the ACF and PACF of the differenced series.
4. Fit the candidates; shortlist on AICc.
5. Residuals white noise? If not, back to step 3.
6. Compare on a holdout, then forecast.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Automatically — the check**

1. Plot the data; transform if needed.
2. `AutoARIMA` chooses $d$, $p$, $q$ and $c$.
3. The same residual check.
4. The same holdout.
:::
::::

Each manual step leaves evidence you can cite in the justification. If `AutoARIMA` lands somewhere
else, the interesting question is **why**.

## Central African Republic exports {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| fig-align: center
diff_car = car.y.diff().dropna()
print("ndiffs:", ndiffs(y_car))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2), width_ratios=[2, 1, 1])
axes[0].plot(car.ds[1:], diff_car, marker="o", markersize=3, color=slate)
axes[0].set_title("First difference of exports, % of GDP")
plot_acf(diff_car, lags=16, zero=False, ax=axes[1], auto_ylims=True)
plot_pacf(diff_car, lags=16, zero=False, ax=axes[2], auto_ylims=True)
plt.show()
```

Two candidate readings: the PACF cuts off at lag 2, which suggests **ARIMA(2,1,0)**. The ACF cuts off at
lag 3, which suggests **ARIMA(0,1,3)**.

## Four candidates {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
candidates = [ARIMA(order=(2, 1, 0), alias="ARIMA(2,1,0)"),
              ARIMA(order=(0, 1, 3), alias="ARIMA(0,1,3)"),
              AutoARIMA(alias="stepwise"),
              AutoARIMA(stepwise=False, alias="full search")]
sf_car = StatsForecast(models=candidates, freq="YS")
sf_car.fit(df=car)
pd.DataFrame([{"model": m.alias, "chosen": str(ARIMASummary(m.model_)).strip(),
               "AICc": m.model_["aicc"], "BIC": m.model_["bic"]}
              for m in sf_car.fitted_[0]]).sort_values("AICc").round(2)
```

Both hand-picked models have a lower AICc than the stepwise search. The full search does slightly
better than all of them, by a margin AICc cannot resolve.

## Residuals: Ljung-Box with the right degrees of freedom {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fit_210 = ARIMA(order=(2, 1, 0)).fit(y=y_car)
resid_210 = fit_210.model_["residuals"]
p, _, q = 2, 1, 0
acorr_ljungbox(resid_210, lags=[10], model_df=p + q)
```

```{python}
#| label: car-residuals
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 2.9), width_ratios=[2, 1, 1])
axes[0].plot(car.ds, resid_210, marker="o", markersize=3, color=orange)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_title("Innovation residuals, ARIMA(2,1,0)")
plot_acf(resid_210, lags=16, zero=False, ax=axes[1], auto_ylims=True)
axes[2].hist(resid_210, bins=15, color=slate)
axes[2].set_title("Histogram")
plt.show()
```

The residuals of an ARIMA($p,d,q$) "spend" $p + q$ degrees of freedom, so the test uses $\ell - p - q$
of them (`model_df`). Here the residuals pass.

## AICc chose. Was it right? {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
benchmarks = [AutoETS(season_length=1, alias="AutoETS"), Naive(alias="naive")]
cv_car = StatsForecast(models=candidates + benchmarks, freq="YS").cross_validation(
    df=car, h=5, n_windows=10, step_size=1)
cv_egy = StatsForecast(
    models=[ARIMA(order=(2, 0, 1), alias="ARIMA(2,0,1)"),
            ARIMA(order=(4, 0, 0), alias="ARIMA(4,0,0)")] + benchmarks,
    freq="YS").cross_validation(df=egypt, h=5, n_windows=10, step_size=1)

score = lambda cv, df: (evaluate(cv.drop(columns="cutoff"),
                                 metrics=[partial(mase, seasonality=1)], train_df=df)
                        .drop(columns=["unique_id", "metric"]).T.round(3))
print("CAR, MASE:"); print(score(cv_car, car).to_string(header=False))
print("\nEgypt, MASE:"); print(score(cv_egy, egypt).to_string(header=False))
```

## AICc chose. Was it right? {.smaller}

- **Egypt:** both ARIMA models beat naive and ETS by a wide margin. ETS can only describe a level and a
  trend, and it has nothing for an 18-year cycle. Of the two ARIMAs, the hand-specified AR(4) does
  slightly better.
- **Central African Republic:** the model with the **lowest AICc forecasts worst**, and naive is
  hard to beat. When the AICc surface is that flat and the series is that short, the choice between
  ARIMA orders is mostly noise.

::: {.callout-important}
The rule from Week 4 does not change with the model family: **AICc shortlists, cross-validation
decides**, and a benchmark goes in every comparison. Sometimes the benchmark wins, and that is an
honest result.
:::

# Forecasting

## Point forecasts {.smaller}

1. Write the model with $y_t$ alone on the left.
2. Replace $t$ by $T + h$.
3. On the right: replace future $y$ by their forecasts, **future errors by zero**, and past errors by
   the residuals $e_t$.

For Egypt's ARIMA(2,0,1):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat y_{T+1|T} &= c + \phi_1 y_T + \phi_2 y_{T-1} + \theta_1 e_T \\
\hat y_{T+2|T} &= c + \phi_1 \hat y_{T+1|T} + \phi_2 y_T \qquad (\theta_1 e_{T+1} \text{ is set to } 0)
\end{aligned}
$$

After $q$ steps the MA part has no information left, and the forecast is driven by the AR part alone.

## By hand, against `predict` {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
y_egy = egypt.y.to_numpy(float)
e = fit_egy.model_["residuals"]
f1 = c + coef["ar1"] * y_egy[-1] + coef["ar2"] * y_egy[-2] + coef["ma1"] * e[-1]
f2 = c + coef["ar1"] * f1 + coef["ar2"] * y_egy[-1]

fc_egy = fit_egy.predict(h=10, level=[95])
print(f"h=1  by hand {f1:.4f}   predict {fc_egy['mean'][0]:.4f}")
print(f"h=2  by hand {f2:.4f}   predict {fc_egy['mean'][1]:.4f}")
```

There is no black box. Once you have the coefficients and the last residual, the forecast is the
recursion written out step by step.

## Prediction intervals {.smaller}

Write the model as an MA($\infty$), $y_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \psi_1\varepsilon_{t-1} +
\psi_2\varepsilon_{t-2} + \cdots$ (the $\psi$ weights from earlier). The $h$-step error is the sum of
the $h$ shocks that have not happened yet:

$$
v_{T+h|T} = \hat\sigma^2\left[1 + \psi_1^2 + \dots + \psi_{h-1}^2\right],
\qquad \hat y_{T+h|T} \pm 1.96\sqrt{v_{T+h|T}}
$$

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
psi = arma2ma([1, -coef["ar1"], -coef["ar2"]], [1, coef["ma1"]], lags=5)
half_width = 1.96 * np.sqrt(fit_egy.model_["sigma2"] * np.cumsum(psi ** 2))
print("from psi weights:", np.round(half_width, 3))
print("from predict:    ", np.round(np.asarray(fc_egy["hi-95"] - fc_egy["mean"])[:5], 3))
```

- $h = 1$: always $\hat\sigma^2$, for every ARIMA.
- MA($q$): $\psi_j = \theta_j$ for $j \le q$ and 0 beyond, so the intervals **stop growing after $q$
  steps**.

## How intervals grow {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: interval-growth
#| fig-align: center
h_show = 30
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.8), sharey=False)
for ax, (name, fit, y_hist, d) in zip(
        axes, [("Egypt, ARIMA(2,0,1)", fit_egy, y_egy, 0), ("CAR, ARIMA(2,1,0)", fit_210, y_car, 1)]):
    fc = fit.predict(h=h_show, level=[80, 95])
    t_h, t_f = np.arange(len(y_hist)), np.arange(len(y_hist), len(y_hist) + h_show)
    ax.plot(t_h, y_hist, color=slate, linewidth=0.9)
    ax.plot(t_f, fc["mean"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8)
    for lvl, a in [(95, 0.12), (80, 0.22)]:
        ax.fill_between(t_f, fc[f"lo-{lvl}"], fc[f"hi-{lvl}"], color=red_pink, alpha=a)
    if d == 0:
        mu_hist, sd_hist = y_hist.mean(), y_hist.std()
        ax.axhline(mu_hist + 1.96 * sd_hist, color=turquoise, linestyle="--", linewidth=1,
                   label="mean ± 1.96 sd of the data")
        ax.axhline(mu_hist - 1.96 * sd_hist, color=turquoise, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
        ax.legend(loc="upper left")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: d = {d}")
plt.show()
```

- $d = 0$: the $\psi$ weights die out, and the interval settles at the **spread of the data itself**.
  Far enough ahead, all the model knows is the unconditional distribution.
- $d \ge 1$: the $\psi$ weights do not die out, and the interval **widens without limit**.

## Why the intervals are too narrow {.smaller}

The formula assumes the residuals are uncorrelated and normal, and it leaves three things out:

- **parameter uncertainty**: $\hat\phi$ and $\hat\theta$ are treated as known;
- **model uncertainty**: the CAR table showed four orders AICc could not separate, and the interval
  uses only one of them;
- **the future resembling the past**: the same structure is assumed to hold over the whole horizon.

In practice, 95% ARIMA intervals often cover less than 95% out of sample. Check the coverage on your
holdout before you defend the intervals.

# ARIMA on a seasonal series

## Non-seasonal ARIMA, monthly data {.smaller}

Your Track B series is seasonal, so this is the case you will meet in practice.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fit_ns = AutoARIMA(season_length=1).fit(y=y_ret)
r_ns = pd.Series(fit_ns.model_["residuals"])
print(ARIMASummary(fit_ns.model_), f"  residual acf at lag 12: {r_ns.autocorr(12):+.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: retail-nonseasonal
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.8))
plot_acf(r_ns, lags=36, zero=False, ax=ax, auto_ylims=True,
         title="Residuals of a non-seasonal ARIMA on monthly retail employment")
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MaxNLocator(integer=True))
plt.show()
```

With `season_length=1` the model has no way to look 12 months back, so the whole season ends up
in the residuals.

## Seasonal difference first, then ARMA {.smaller}

Do what the tests said: one seasonal difference, then let the non-seasonal part model the rest.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fit_sd = AutoARIMA(season_length=12, max_P=0, max_Q=0).fit(y=y_ret)
r_sd = pd.Series(fit_sd.model_["residuals"])
print(ARIMASummary(fit_sd.model_), f"\nresidual acf at lag 12: {r_sd.autocorr(12):+.2f}\n")

cv_ret = StatsForecast(
    models=[AutoARIMA(season_length=1, alias="non-seasonal"),
            AutoARIMA(season_length=12, max_P=0, max_Q=0, alias="D=1 + ARMA"),
            SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, alias="snaive")],
    freq="MS").cross_validation(df=retail, h=12, n_windows=5, step_size=12)
evaluate(cv_ret.drop(columns="cutoff"), metrics=[partial(mase, seasonality=12)],
         train_df=retail).round(3)
```

`max_P=0, max_Q=0` lets `AutoARIMA` take a seasonal difference but adds no seasonal AR or MA terms.
In other words, it uses only today's material.

## What is still left {.smaller}

- The non-seasonal model **loses to seasonal naive**. The seasonal difference plus an ARMA **beats it
  clearly**.
- The residual autocorrelation at lag 12 is still `{python} f"{r_sd.autocorr(12):+.2f}"`. Seasonal
  differencing over-corrects slightly, and that is the same over-differencing signature you saw at lag
  1, now at lag 12.
- The fix is a **seasonal MA term**, a $\Theta_1\varepsilon_{t-12}$. That is ARIMA$(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_m$,
  next week.

::: {.callout-note}
We ran the same three-way comparison on all 140 issued Track B series. Non-seasonal ARIMA beats the
benchmark on **14%** of them, seasonal difference + ARMA on **60%**, and full seasonal `AutoARIMA` on
**all** of them, which the pool screen guarantees. Seasonal differencing gets you most of the way, and
part 2 covers the rest.
:::

# ARIMA in practice

## Five ways to get this wrong {.smaller}

| Trap | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Comparing AICc across different $d$ | A "better" model that is fitted to different data | Fix $d$ with the tests first, then compare $p$ and $q$ |
| Over-differencing | A large negative spike at lag 1 (or $m$) in the differenced ACF | Go back one difference |
| Reading `intercept` as $c$ | The equation does not reproduce the forecasts | `statsforecast` reports the mean, so $c = \mu(1 - \sum\phi_i)$ |
| Ljung-Box with `model_df=0` | Residuals look whiter than they are | `model_df = p + q` |
| `season_length=1` on seasonal data | Residual ACF spike at lag $m$, and the model loses to `snaive` | Seasonal difference, then the seasonal terms from part 2 |

## What ARIMA is, in one slide {.smaller}

- **Is:** a model of the series' **autocorrelation**. Differencing removes what does not stay put, and
  AR and MA terms describe what is left.
- **Is:** a family that contains naive, drift, mean and SES as special cases, so the Week 1
  benchmarks are ARIMA models that were never estimated.
- **Is:** something you can specify by hand from evidence (tests, ACF, PACF) and check automatically.
  When the two disagree you learn something either way.
- **Is not:** interpretable in terms of trend and season the way ETS is. An ARIMA(2,0,1) does not
  have a "level" you can plot.
- **Is not:** finished on seasonal data yet. That is part 2.

## In the practice session {.smaller}

**Today's practice** is the worked example for **Challenge 2: ETS** on your own series, from the Week 4
lecture. The ARIMA material from today goes into **next week's** practice and Challenge 3.

For Challenge 3 the justification block asks you to **specify the model by hand first**:

1. choose $D$ and $d$ from the tests and the plots, and show both;
2. read $p$ and $q$ from the ACF and PACF of the differenced series, and name the lags you used;
3. check the residuals with Ljung-Box and the right `model_df`;
4. only then run `AutoARIMA`, and explain any difference from your choice.
